title: Gandhi's farewell: love the smallest
hookLine: not-harming as a blank, or with a heart in it; the week looked back
tomorrow: so how does a man of nonviolence live by a war book?
last: HOLD FIRM TO TRUTH, WITHOUT HATE.

lines: A FORM WITH EVERY BOX EMPTY.
cards: Not-harming can sound like a blank: don't hit, don't shout, don't do anything. A form with every box left empty. Gandhi read it the other way.
At the very end of his autobiography, in a short farewell, he says what he thinks is inside it. Not a rule about what to avoid, but something to reach for.

teach.b: The word is ahimsa, not-harming. In the farewell he writes, in paraphrase, that to see the Spirit of Truth face to face, a person has to be able to love the smallest creature as oneself.
And he calls ahimsa the farthest edge of humility. So for Gandhi, not-harming wasn't empty. It had a heart in it: care, reaching even toward the person you oppose.
You stand firm, you don't move, and you still wish the other side well. It's harder than staying quiet, and harder than shouting.
Now look back down the road of this week. A guest who sailed home to serve God in the poor. A sutra that makes posture a steady, easy seat.
Arjuna's question, sit apart or act, and karma yoga. A stairway of poses toward a still mind. Kaushika's harmful truth, and ahimsa before the first pose.
And holding firm to truth without hatred, from a Hindu lawyer to a Baptist pastor.
Two weeks of ideas leaving India, and meeting people on the way.

how: Readers of Gandhi often turn to the farewell at the end of his autobiography, where he ties truth, ahimsa and humility together.

two leaders who disagreed about whether to resist

to see Truth, love the smallest creature as oneself.

games.q: you're protesting a school rule you think is unfair, and the principal walks past. by Gandhi's farewell, what's inside your stand?
o: stand firm and let her see you're angry.
step aside; not-harming means not protesting.
stand firm, and still wish her well.
games.why: for Gandhi, not-harming has love in it: you hold your ground and still wish the other side well.

practice: Count on your fingers the people who've shown you a kindness they didn't have to, one finger for each face. When you run out of fingers, or faces, rest your hands open in your lap and stay with them.
